Fix $y$ . For each reference point $\widetilde{x}$ , Proposition A.1 shows that the fixed-reference position operator $\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}\mathsf{T}_{\pi}^{y,\widetilde{x}}\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}^{*}$ is a self-adjoint Markov contraction on $L^{2}(\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y})$ . The reference point in Algorithm 1 is drawn independently from $\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}$ . Consequently, the conditional half-turn operator is the average $(\mathsf{H}_{y}f)(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}} igl(\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}\mathsf{T}_{\pi}^{y,\widetilde{x}}\mathsf{\Pi}_{p}^{*}f igr)(x)\,\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}(\mathrm{d}\widetilde{x})\,.$ The averaging measure does not depend on $x$ , so $\mathsf{H}_{y}$ is again a self-adjoint Markov contraction. In kernel form, this is the detailed-balance identity $\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}(\mathrm{d}x)\,\mathcal{H}_{y}(x,\mathrm{d}x^{\prime})=\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}(\mathrm{d}x^{\prime})\,\mathcal{H}_{y}(x^{\prime},\mathrm{d}x)\,,$ which proves the proposition. ∎ The preceding reversibility statement holds for each fixed $y$ . To use these kernels as a single operator on the augmented space, we next verify their joint measurability and then integrate the conditional operator identities over $y$ . Proposition A.2 (Joint measurability and augmented space half-turn operator) . The family of conditional half-turn kernels $(\mathcal{H}_{y})_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}$ admits a version, again denoted by $\mathcal{H}_{y}(x,\mathrm{d}x^{\prime})$ , such that $(y,x)\mapsto\mathcal{H}_{y}(x,A)$ is Borel measurable for every Borel set $A\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . Consequently, $(\mathsf{H}f)(x,y)\coloneqq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(x^{\prime},y)\,\mathcal{H}_{y}(x,\mathrm{d}x^{\prime})$ (A.9) defines a self-adjoint Markov contraction on $L^{2}(\pi_{\eta})$ . Proof. Since $
abla V$ is continuous, the harmonic flow, event rate, and reflection map are jointly Borel; the convention $R_{0}=I$ ensures this even where the reflection normal vanishes. The integrated hazard is jointly Borel, with continuous, nondecreasing dependence on time, so its threshold-crossing times are Borel, as can be checked using rational times. Thus the recursion ( A.1 )–( A.2 ) makes each jump time and post-jump state Borel in $(y,x_{0},p_{0},\widetilde{x},(E_{j})_{j\geq 1})$ . By non-explosion, the terminal state at time $\pi$ is the almost-sure limit of the Borel terminal states obtained by allowing at most $n$ jumps. Setting the limit to zero wherever it does not exist gives a Borel version. The conditional density in ( 2.8 ) is jointly Borel in $(y,\widetilde{x})$ . Integrating $\mathbf{1}_{\{x_{\pi}\in A\}}$ against this reference law and the laws of the Gaussian momentum and exponential clocks therefore makes $(y,x)\mapsto\mathcal{H}_{y}(x,A)$ Borel for every Borel set $A$ . Finally, each $\mathsf{H}_{y}$ is a self-adjoint Markov contraction by Proposition 3.2 . Integrating the conditional contraction bound gives $\displaystyle\|\mathsf{H}f\|_{L^{2}(\pi_{\eta})}^{2}$ $\displaystyle\leq\int igl\|f(\cdot,y) igr\|_{L^{2}(\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y})}^{2}\,\pi_{\eta}^{Y}(\mathrm{d}y)=\|f\|_{L^{2}(\pi_{\eta})}^{2}\,.$ Conditional self-adjointness and Fubini likewise give $\langle f,\mathsf{H}gangle=\langle\mathsf{H}f,gangle$ for bounded measurable $f,g$ , and hence for all $L^{2}(\pi_{\eta})$ by density. Positivity and $\mathsf{H}1=1$ follow from the corresponding properties of each $\mathsf{H}_{y}$ . ∎ <section id="A1.SS3" class

text: B.1 Operator framework and micro–macro decomposition Our target distribution is the joint law $\pi_{\eta}$ defined in ( 2.6 ), and we set $\mathfrak{H}\coloneqq L^{2}(\pi_{\eta})$ . Recall from ( 3.11 ) that the ideal Proximal BPS has transition kernel $\mathcal{K}\bigl((x,y),\mathrm{d}x^{\prime}\,\mathrm{d}y^{\prime}\bigr)=\delta_{2x-y}(\mathrm{d}y^{\prime})\,\bigl[\rho\,\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y^{\prime}}(\mathrm{d}x^{\prime})+(1-\rho)\,\mathcal{H}_{y^{\prime}}(x,\mathrm{d}x^{\prime})\bigr]\,,$ where $\mathcal{H}_{y^{\prime}}$ is the conditional half-turn kernel from Proposition 3.2 . Since the algorithm is a discrete-time chain, its evolution is described by the induced one-step Markov operator on observables, $(\mathsf{K}f)(x,y)\coloneqq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d}}f(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\,\mathcal{K}\bigl((x,y),\mathrm{d}x^{\prime}\,\mathrm{d}y^{\prime}\bigr)\,.$ Thus $\mathcal{K}$ acts on probability laws, whereas $\mathsf{K}$ is its induced action on observables. The first term in brackets in $\mathcal{K}$ is the conditional resampling branch. After the auxiliary coordinate is updated to $y^{\prime}$ , this branch replaces the $x$ -coordinate by an independent draw from $\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y^{\prime}}$ . The associated conditional expectation operator is $(\mathsf{P}f)(x,y)\coloneqq\int f(x^{\prime},y)\,\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}(\mathrm{d}x^{\prime})=\mathbb{E}[f(X,Y)\mid Y=y]\,.$ (B.1) In particular, $\mathsf{P}f$ depends only on the coordinate $y$ . The range and kernel of $\mathsf{P}$ are $\begin{split}\mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}}&\coloneqq\operatorname{ran}(\mathsf{P})=\{f\in\mathfrak{H}:f(x,y)=g(y)\text{ for some }g\in L^{2}(\pi_{\eta}^{Y})\}\,,\\ \mathfrak{H}_{\perp}&\coloneqq\ker(\mathsf{P})=\operatorname{ran}(\mathsf{P}^{\perp})=\{f\in\mathfrak{H}:\mathbb{E}[f(X,Y)\mid Y]=0\}\,.\end{split}$ (B.2) Here $\mathsf{P}^{\perp}\coloneqq I-\mathsf{P}$ , so $\mathfrak{H}=\mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}}\oplus\mathfrak{H}_{\perp}$ and $f=\mathsf{P}f+\mathsf{P}^{\perp}f$ . In the common terminology of hypocoercivity [ 14 , 21 ] , $\operatorname{ran}(\mathsf{P})$ is the macroscopic subspace and its orthogonal complement is the microscopic subspace. Thus functions in $\mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}}$ depend only on the coordinate $y$ , whereas functions in $\mathfrak{H}_{\perp}$ have zero mean under $\pi_{\eta}^{X\mid Y=y}$ for $\pi_{\eta}^{Y}$ -almost every $y$ . Relative to the decomposition $\mathfrak{H}=\mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}}\oplus\mathfrak{H}_{\perp}$ , we write an operator $\mathsf{T}$ on $\mathfrak{H}$ in block form as $\mathsf{T}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathsf{T}_{\mathsf{P}\mathsf{P}}&\mathsf{T}_{\mathsf{P}\perp}\\ \mathsf{T}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}&\mathsf{T}_{\perp\perp}\end{pmatrix}\,,\hskip 20.00003pt\begin{aligned} \mathsf{T}_{\mathsf{P}\mathsf{P}}&\coloneqq\mathsf{P}\mathsf{T}\mathsf{P}\,,&\mathsf{T}_{\mathsf{P}\perp}&\coloneqq\mathsf{P}\mathsf{T}\mathsf{P}^{\perp}\,,\\ \mathsf{T}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}&\coloneqq\mathsf{P}^{\perp}\mathsf{T}\mathsf{P}\,,&\mathsf{T}_{\perp\perp}&\coloneqq\mathsf{P}^{\perp}\mathsf{T}\mathsf{P}^{\perp}\,.\end{aligned}$ (B.3) The first subscript specifies the target subspace and the second the source subspace; thus $\mathsf{T}_{ab}:\mathfrak{H}_{b}\to\mathfrak{H}_{a}$ for $a,b\in\{\mathsf{P},\perp\}$ . We first apply this block notation to the reflection map $\mathsf{U}$ from ( 2.14 ). We use the same symbol for its pullback on observables: $(\mathsf{U}f)(x,y)\coloneqq f(\mathsf{U}(x,y))=f(x,2x-y)\,.$ (B.4) This pullback is self-adjoint and unitary, and hence has block matrix $\mathsf{U}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{P}\mathsf{P}}&\mathsf{U}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}^{*}\\ \mathsf{U}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}&\mathsf{U}_{\perp\perp}\end{pmatrix}\,.$ Here $\mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{P}\mathsf{P}}=\mathsf{P}\mathsf{U}\mathsf{P}$ maps $\mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}}$ to itself, whereas $\mathsf{U}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}=\mathsf{P}^{\perp}\mathsf{U}\mathsf{P}$ maps $\mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}}$ to $\mathfrak{H}_{\perp}$ . Since $\mathsf{U}$ is self-adjoint and unitary, $\mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{P}\mathsf{P}}$ is a self-adjoint contraction on $\mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}}$ . Writing $\mathsf{U}^{2}=I$ in blocks gives $\mathsf{U}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}^{*}\mathsf{U}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}=I-\mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{P}\mathsf{P}}^{2}\,,\hskip 20.00003pt\mathsf{U}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}^{*}\mathsf{U}_{\perp\perp}=-\mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{P}\mathsf{P}}\mathsf{U}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}^{*}\,.$ (B.5) We next express the joint half-turn operator $\mathsf{H}$ in the same block decomposition. It is defined in ( A.9 ) and is a self-adjoint Markov contraction by Proposition A.2 . Since $\mathsf{H}$ acts only on the $x$ -coordinate, while every function in $\operatorname{ran}(\mathsf{P})$ depends only on $y$ , we have $\mathsf{H}\mathsf{P}=\mathsf{P}$ . Self-adjointness also gives $\mathsf{P}\mathsf{H}=\mathsf{P}$ . Set $\mathsf{H}_{\perp\perp}\coloneqq\mathsf{P}^{\perp}\mathsf{H}\mathsf{P}^{\perp}:\mathfrak{H}_{\perp}\to\mathfrak{H}_{\perp}$ . The identity $\mathsf{P}\mathsf{H}=\mathsf{P}$ makes $\mathfrak{H}_{\perp}$ invariant under $\mathsf{H}$ , so $\mathsf{H}_{\perp\perp}$ is its restriction to $\mathfrak{H}_{\perp}$ . It is therefore self-adjoint, and $\|\mathsf{H}_{\perp\perp}g\|=\|\mathsf{H}g\|\leq\|g\|$ for $g\in\mathfrak{H}_{\perp}$ . Consequently, $\mathsf{H}=\mathsf{P}+\mathsf{H}_{\perp\perp}\,,\hskip 20.00003pt-I\preceq\mathsf{H}_{\perp\perp}\preceq I\hskip 10.00002pt\text{on }\mathfrak{H}_{\perp}\,.$ (B.6) Relative to $\mathfrak{H}=\mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}}\oplus\mathfrak{H}_{\perp}$ , this decomposition has the block representation $\mathsf{H}=\begin{pmatrix}I_{\mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}}}&0\\ 0&\mathsf{H}_{\perp\perp}\end{pmatrix}\,.$ The Markov operator $\mathsf{K}$ induced by the transition kernel $\mathcal{K}$ therefore factors as $\mathsf{K}=\mathsf{U}\bigl[\rho\mathsf{P}+(1-\rho)\mathsf{H}\bigr]=\mathsf{U}\bigl[\mathsf{P}+(1-\rho)\mathsf{H}_{\perp\perp}\bigr]\,.$ (B.7) Accordingly, its block representation is $\mathsf{K}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{P}\mathsf{P}}&\mathsf{U}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}^{*}\\ \mathsf{U}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}&\mathsf{U}_{\perp\perp}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}I_{\mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}}}&0\\ 0&(1-\rho)\mathsf{H}_{\perp\perp}\end{pmatrix}\,.$ The diagonal factor in the block representation of $\mathsf{K}$ contracts $\mathfrak{H}_{\perp}$ but leaves $\mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}}$ unchanged. For an observable $f\in\mathfrak{H}_{\mathsf{P}}$ , contraction therefore relies on the $\mathfrak{H}_{\perp}$ -component $\mathsf{U}_{\perp\mathsf{P}}f$ created by reflection. The next subsection estimates this component and the subsequent action of $\mathsf{H}_{\perp\perp}$ .
